question: What proportion of adults at high risk from sepsis (NEWS2 7 or more with suspected infection) receive IV antibiotics within 1 hour of their first ED NEWS2 score?
why: NG253 (2025, updated 2026) fixes time zero as the first ED NEWS2 score. Library sepsis audits used older bundles and screening tools [3007][2618]; none measures the 1-hour limit from the NEWS2 time stamp.

standard.wording: Give people aged 16 or over who are at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic treatment, within 1 hour of calculating the person's NEWS2 score on initial assessment in the emergency department or on ward deterioration. Only give antibiotics if they have not been given before for this episode of sepsis (see recommendations 1.7.7 and 1.7.8 on managing the condition while awaiting transfer).

pass: First IV antibiotic dose recorded as given on the drug chart within 60 minutes of the first ED NEWS2 time; or pre-hospital antibiotics already given for this episode.
population: Adults 16 or over with suspected or confirmed infection and a first ED NEWS2 of 7 or more. Exclude end-of-life care plans and patients who left before treatment.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible ED attendances over the last 2 months.
data_source: ED system or e-observations for first NEWS2 time; EPMA or drug chart for antibiotic administration time; ambulance record for pre-hospital antibiotics.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Build an automatic ED alert on the e-observations system: a NEWS2 of 7 or more with an 'infection suspected' tick opens a sepsis order set with a pre-filled antibiotic and a 60-minute countdown on the tracking board.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible attendances, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED governance and the Trust deteriorating patient group. If it works, keep the alert in the e-observations build and report monthly to the sepsis lead.
evidence: [3007] paediatric severe sepsis: antibiotics within 1 hour 42% at baseline (no standard met)
[1847] delirium: compulsory electronic screen raised completion 3% → 87% (system change beats teaching)
[1358] ED VTE assessment: electronic discharge prompt 32% → 93.1% (electronic prompt)
pitfalls: Time zero recorded differently between cycles → agree in advance that time zero is the first ED NEWS2 time stamp, not triage or doctor review.
Prescription time used instead of administration time → take only the 'given' time from EPMA.
Medium-risk patients with a 3-point single parameter caused by infection are missed → add a column and decide inclusion rules before cycle 1.
Nursing staff see the audit as blame → share results by shift pattern, not by name.
Gains fade after rotation → make the alert part of the system, not a poster.
pearls: Recruit the ED sepsis nurse and the EPR analyst on day 1; they can pull NEWS2 time stamps in bulk.
Record the reason for each delay; the commonest cause tells you which fix to pick.
Use a run chart of weekly compliance, not a single percentage.
Hand the monthly report to a consultant owner before you rotate.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from e-observations and EPMA

question: What proportion of adults at high risk from sepsis who receive IV fluid in the ED are given an initial bolus of 250 ml?
why: NG253 (2025) cut the first sepsis bolus from 500 ml to 250 ml with reassessment after each bolus. Old habits and pre-printed sepsis stickers still say 500 ml. No audit of bolus volume is published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.6 and 1.8.8 (November 2025, updated September 2026)
standard.wording: 1.8.6 Give an initial bolus of 250 ml. Ideally, give this over 10 to 15 minutes. [2025] ... 1.8.8 Reassess after each fluid bolus. [2025]

pass: First resuscitation bolus prescribed and given as 250 ml of crystalloid, with a documented reassessment (observations or clinical note) before any further bolus.
population: Adults 16 or over at high risk from sepsis (NEWS2 7 or more, or medium risk with hypoperfusion) given IV fluid resuscitation in the ED. Exclude patients in cardiac arrest.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible attendances over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: EPMA or fluid chart for volume and time; e-observations and clinical notes for reassessment.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Pass criterion 2; 'not applicable' if one bolus only

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Replace the sepsis order set default from '500 ml bolus' to '250 ml over 10–15 minutes, reassess' and reprint the sepsis sticker with the same wording.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED and acute medicine governance. If it works, lock the new default into the order set and add it to the ED induction pack.
evidence: [1517] arthroplasty analgesia: electronic order set raised full protocol compliance 0/27 → 58% (order set default)
[2471] ED renal colic: renal order set lifted NSAID use 54.5% → 71.9% (order set)
[2196] emergency surgery VTE doses: two checkboxes added to the drug chart, correct dosing 29/36 → 37/38 (chart redesign)
pitfalls: Old 500 ml bags or stickers left in resus → remove old stock labels and stickers on the change date.
Paramedic pre-alert fluids counted as the first bolus → record pre-hospital fluid separately.
Clinicians object that 250 ml is too little in shock → share the NG253 wording and stress repeat boluses up to 1,000 ml.
Reassessment not written down → accept a timed set of observations as reassessment.
pearls: Agree definitions with the ED sepsis lead before cycle 1.
Ask pharmacy to change the order set default; it is quick and lasts beyond rotation.
Pair the audit with the antibiotic timing audit to share data collection.
Report total fluid in the first hour too, to show no one is under-resuscitated.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPMA and fluid chart

question: What proportion of adults at medium risk from sepsis (NEWS2 5 or 6 with suspected infection) are reviewed by an FY2-level or more senior clinician, with the venous lactate result, within 1 hour?
why: NG253 (2024, amended 2026) allows antibiotics to be deferred up to 3 hours for medium-risk patients only if a competent clinician reviews them and the lactate within 1 hour. No library audit covers the medium-risk group.

standard.wording: For people aged 16 or over with a medium risk of severe illness or death from sepsis: carry out a venous blood test, including for: blood gas, including glucose and lactate measurement ... arrange for a clinician with core competencies in the care of acutely ill patients (FY2 level or above) to review the person's condition and venous lactate results within 1 hour of the person being assessed as at medium risk. [2024, amended 2026]

pass: A timed clinical note by an FY2 or more senior clinician, mentioning the lactate result, within 60 minutes of the first NEWS2 of 5 or 6.
population: Adults 16 or over with suspected infection and a first ED NEWS2 of 5 or 6. Exclude patients who became high risk before review.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible attendances over the last 2 months.
data_source: E-observations for NEWS2 time; blood gas analyser or lab system for lactate time; ED notes for reviewer grade and time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'medium sepsis risk' flag to the ED tracking board that starts a 60-minute timer and prompts an automatic venous gas at triage.
close_loop: Present at ED governance. If it works, keep the flag and include medium-risk review in the monthly sepsis dashboard.
evidence: [3007] paediatric sepsis: lactate done 89% but timed care standards all missed (timing is the gap)
[2174] ED frailty: mandatory field in ED software raised CFS recording 40% → 100% (system change)
[1781] delirium: stickers and emails peaked then fell to 1.3% by week 6 (paper prompts fade)
pitfalls: Grade of reviewer not recorded → use the rota or login name to confirm grade.
Lactate done on the arterial gas instead → accept any blood gas lactate.
Patients escalate to high risk and drop out → record them and analyse separately.
Night-time staffing skews results → report by time of day.
pearls: Get the ED nurse in charge to agree triage-led venous gas before cycle 1.
Pull NEWS2 5–6 plus infection codes from the EPR to find cases fast.
Record the antibiotic decision to show safe deferral, not just speed.
Present results with the high-risk antibiotic audit as one sepsis story.

question: What proportion of children under 16 with suspected sepsis who meet a NICE high risk criterion receive antibiotics within 1 hour of meeting that criterion in the ED?
why: NG254 (2025) keeps the 1-hour antibiotic limit for high-risk children. The library shows antibiotics within 1 hour in only 42% [3007] and a local paperwork redesign without published figures [279].

standard.wording: Ensure urgent assessment mechanisms are in place to deliver antibiotics when any high risk criteria are met in a person under 16 in secondary care (within 1 hour of meeting a high risk criterion in an acute hospital setting). [2016]

pass: First antibiotic dose given (IV or IO) within 60 minutes of the first recorded high risk criterion.
population: Children under 16 attending the ED with suspected sepsis and at least one NG254 high risk criterion. Exclude those given antibiotics before arrival.
sample: 30–40 consecutive eligible children over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: Paediatric ED notes and PEWS charts for criterion time; EPMA or drug chart for antibiotic time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a paediatric sepsis 'grab box' with pre-drawn antibiotic doses by weight band and an IO needle, and a sepsis flag on the PEWS chart that starts a 60-minute timer.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 (or next 3 months if numbers are small), same template.
close_loop: Present at the paediatric and ED joint governance meeting. If it works, include the box check in the daily resus checklist.
evidence: [3007] paediatric severe sepsis: antibiotics within 1 hour 42%, fluids within 1 hour 42%
[279] children's ED sepsis: paperwork redesign after gaps found (form change)
[1974] ED trauma: dedicated booklet raised secondary survey documentation 50% → 87.5% (form)
pitfalls: Small numbers in a DGH → extend the look-back to 6 months or share with a neighbouring ED.
Criterion time hard to find → use the first PEWS chart entry showing the criterion.
Cannulation delays blamed → record access method and attempts.
Paediatric and ED teams dispute ownership → run it as a joint audit with named leads from each.
pearls: Recruit a paediatric nurse champion to check the grab box daily.
Use the ED coding for 'sepsis' and 'fever' to find cases.
Agree what counts as the criterion time before cycle 1.
Give weight-band dosing cards to reduce prescribing delay.

question: What proportion of febrile infants under 3 months seen in the ED have all four NICE baseline tests (full blood count, blood culture, CRP and urine)?
why: Infants under 3 months with fever are high risk. Missed urine samples and cultures are common. The library has only a local registered re-audit on infant fever sign-off [451]; no audit of the NICE test set.

standard.wording: Perform the following investigations in infants younger than 3 months with fever: full blood count; blood culture; C-reactive protein; urine testing for urinary tract infection (see the sections on urine collection, preservation and testing in the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection in under 16s)

pass: FBC, blood culture, CRP and a urine sample for UTI testing all sent during the ED or assessment unit stay.
population: Infants under 3 months (corrected age) with a measured temperature of 38°C or higher. Exclude transfers already investigated elsewhere.
sample: 30–40 consecutive infants over the last 6 months.
data_source: ED system for cases; lab system for tests sent; notes for temperature.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Create a 'febrile infant under 3 months' order set in the EPR that requests all four tests in one click, with a urine bag or clean-catch kit added to the ED triage pack.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14, then monthly until 30 infants re-audited.
close_loop: Present at paediatric governance. If it works, keep the order set and add a urine check to the paediatric handover sheet.
evidence: [451] local re-audit: consultant sign-off for fever in infants under one (registered)
[2471] ED renal colic: renal order set raised calcium requests 77.9% → 94.7% (order set)
[2970] paediatric antimicrobials: weekly feedback lifted guideline compliance 30% → 100% (feedback plus guideline)
pitfalls: Urine sent but not labelled as from the ED → search by date and hospital number.
Temperature of 38°C measured only at home → decide in advance whether to include parental reports.
Small numbers → extend look-back and run a monthly run chart.
Urine collection is slow and staff give up → add a clean-catch technique card.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric registrar lead and a play specialist for urine collection tips.
Report each test separately so you know which one fails.
Link the order set to the NG254 parenteral antibiotic rule for under 1 month.
Keep a one-page summary for new starters.
effort: ~15 min per 10 infants from lab system

question: What proportion of children under 5 with fever seen in the ED have temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and capillary refill time all recorded at first assessment?
why: The traffic light system depends on all four measures, and capillary refill time is the one most often left out. The library has no audit of NG143 routine assessment in the ED.

standard.wording: Measure and record temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and capillary refill time as part of the routine assessment of a child with fever. [2007]

pass: All four values recorded in the triage or first clinician observations.
population: Children aged 0–5 years attending the ED with fever as the presenting complaint. Exclude major trauma and cardiac arrest.
sample: 50 consecutive attendances over 2 weeks.
data_source: ED system triage observations and PEWS chart.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make capillary refill time a mandatory field in the paediatric triage screen on the ED system (cannot save without it).
close_loop: Present to the ED nursing team and paediatric governance. If it works, keep the mandatory field and add CRT to the PEWS chart review.
evidence: [2174] ED frailty: mandatory CFS field in ED software raised recording 40% → 100% (mandatory field)
[1847] delirium: obligatory electronic screen 3% → 87% (mandatory field)
[3007] paediatric sepsis: vital signs within 15 minutes 47% at baseline
pitfalls: Triage staff resist more mandatory fields → agree with the nurse lead and show baseline data first.
CRT entered as '<2' by default → check for copy-forward values.
Only initial observations audited → keep to first assessment to avoid mixed definitions.
Streamed children seen in UTC are missed → include UTC or state exclusion.
pearls: Recruit a paediatric ED nurse to co-lead.
Collect traffic light category too; it adds value at no extra time.
Show missing CRT by time of day to target training.
A mandatory field keeps working after rotation.
effort: ~10 min per 10 children from triage screen

question: What proportion of adults with a head injury and a NICE 1-hour CT risk factor have their CT head scan within 1 hour of that risk factor being identified?
why: NG232 (2023) sets a 1-hour limit for high-risk adults. The library head injury work measured neurosurgical advice time [2101] and c-spine imaging in older adults [1147]; none measures the 1-hour CT limit.

standard.wording: For people 16 and over who have sustained a head injury, do a CT head scan within 1 hour of any of these risk factors being identified: a GCS score of 12 or less on initial assessment in the emergency department; a GCS score of less than 15 at 2 hours after the injury on assessment in the emergency department; suspected open or depressed skull fracture; any sign of basal skull fracture (haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the ear or nose, Battle's sign); post-traumatic seizure; focal neurological deficit; more than 1 episode of vomiting. [2023]

pass: CT acquisition time within 60 minutes of the first documented risk factor time.
population: Adults 16 or over with head injury and at least one rec 1.5.8 risk factor. Exclude patients already scanned elsewhere.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ED notes for risk factor and time; PACS/RIS for request and scan times.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Introduce a 'NICE 1-hour head CT' request option on the radiology system that flags as urgent on the CT worklist and alerts the radiographer by bleep.
close_loop: Present jointly at ED and radiology governance. If it works, keep the request category and report monthly on the CT dashboard.
evidence: [2101] DGH head injury: proforma introduced; median time to neurosurgical advice 229 minutes
[2612] trauma calls: ED trauma lead each shift cut silver trauma imaging time 6 h 29 min → 3 h 21 min
[1147] older head injury: posters raised CT c-spine 16% → 38% but documentation stayed 16% (posters alone limited)
pitfalls: Risk factor time is not written → use the first note describing it and record how often it is missing.
Radiology feels blamed → run it jointly with a radiology lead.
Request made late, not scan late → record request time to split ED and radiology delay.
Changing inclusion between cycles → use the same list of 7 risk factors.
pearls: Get CT acquisition times in bulk from RIS.
Split the timeline into identify → request → scan → report.
Recruit a CT superintendent radiographer early.
Show the worst delays as short case stories at governance.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from notes and RIS

question: What proportion of adults on anticoagulants with a head injury and no other CT indication have a documented CT decision with a reason?
why: NG232 (2023) changed anticoagulated head injury from 'scan all' to 'consider CT within 8 hours'. Many EDs still scan by habit or discharge without a recorded decision. No audit of this change is published in the library.

standard.wording: For people who have sustained a head injury and have no other indications for a CT head scan, but are on anticoagulant treatment (including vitamin K antagonists, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin and low molecular weight heparins) or antiplatelet treatment (excluding aspirin monotherapy), consider doing a CT head scan: within 8 hours of the injury (for example, if it is difficult to do a risk assessment or if the person might not return to the emergency department if they have signs of deterioration) or within the hour if they present more than 8 hours after the injury.

pass: Notes record a CT decision (scan or no scan) and a reason; if scanned, CT within 8 hours of injury (or within 1 hour if presenting after 8 hours).
population: Adults 16 or over on anticoagulant or non-aspirin antiplatelet therapy with head injury and no rec 1.5.8 or 1.5.9 risk factors.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2 months.
data_source: ED notes and medication history; RIS for CT times.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an 'anticoagulated head injury' box to the ED head injury proforma asking: CT yes/no, reason (difficult assessment, unable to return, other) and time of injury.
close_loop: Present at ED governance with the scan yield. If it works, keep the proforma box and share the yield data with radiology.
evidence: [1147] older head injury imaging: posters raised CT c-spine 16% → 38% (education alone limited)
[2093] hand trauma: electronic proforma improved 11/15 data points (proforma)
[2101] DGH head injury: head injury proforma plus elderly care input (proforma)
pitfalls: Patients with other risk factors slip in → screen each case against recs 1.5.8 and 1.5.9 first.
Aspirin alone included by mistake → exclude aspirin monotherapy.
Clinicians fear missing a bleed → present yield and the NICE rationale together.
Injury time missing → record 'unknown' and treat as presenting after 8 hours.
pearls: Pull cases from the ED head injury code plus medication list.
Report the CT yield; it helps the department agree a local stance.
Get a consultant to sign off the proforma wording.
Keep the box short so it gets used.

question: What proportion of children with a head injury and exactly one NICE risk factor are observed for at least 4 hours from the time of injury?
why: NG232 (2023) asks for 4 hours of observation when a child has only one rec 1.5.11 risk factor. Early discharge is common in busy EDs. No library audit covers paediatric head injury observation.

standard.wording: Observe people under 16 who have sustained a head injury but have only 1 of the risk factors in recommendation 1.5.11 for a minimum of 4 hours from the time of injury. If, during observation, any of the following risk factors are identified, do a CT head scan within 1 hour: a GCS score of less than 15; further vomiting; a further episode of abnormal drowsiness. If none of these risk factors occur during observation, use clinical judgement to determine whether a longer period of observation is needed. [2023]

pass: Documented observations continue until at least 4 hours after the time of injury before discharge.
population: Children under 16 with head injury and exactly one rec 1.5.11 risk factor and no rec 1.5.10 factor.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible children over the last 3 months.
data_source: Paediatric head injury proforma, PEWS and neuro-observation chart, ED discharge time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'discharge not before' time box to the paediatric head injury proforma, calculated as injury time plus 4 hours, and show it on the tracking board.
close_loop: Present at paediatric and ED governance. If it works, keep the box and add it to the children's ED induction.
evidence: [1974] ED trauma: dedicated booklet raised documentation 50% → 87.5% (form)
[2093] hand trauma: electronic proforma improved 11/15 data points (proforma)
[1781] delirium: sticker use fell from 57% to 0% by week 6 (stickers alone fade)
pitfalls: Injury time not recorded → make it a required field; record 'unknown' in cycle 1.
Children observed in a separate area with paper charts → check both paper and electronic records.
Breach pressure pushes early discharge → share with the site team that observation counts as care.
Multi-factor children included by mistake → screen for 1.5.10 and 1.5.11 factors first.
pearls: Recruit a paediatric ED nurse to check the 'discharge not before' box.
Report deterioration during observation to show why the rule matters.
Use the tracking board so the time is visible to all.
Agree the proforma change with the paediatric lead before cycle 1.

question: What proportion of children discharged from the ED after a head injury have a letter sent to their GP and to their health visitor or school nurse within 48 hours?
why: NG232 asks for a GP letter within 48 hours shared with health visitors or school nurses. This is a safeguarding safety net. Only a local registered re-audit of GP letters for children exists in the library [449].

standard.wording: For anyone who has attended the emergency department with a head injury, write to their GP within 48 hours of discharge, giving details of clinical history and examination. Also share this letter with health visitors (for preschool children) and school nurses (for school-age children and young people). If appropriate, provide a copy of the letter for the person with a head injury, and their family or carers, custodial staff or social worker. [2014]

pass: GP letter sent within 48 hours of ED discharge and copied to the health visitor (under 5) or school nurse (school age).
population: Children under 16 discharged home from the ED after a head injury.
sample: 50 consecutive discharges over 2–4 weeks.
data_source: ED system discharge letter log (sent time and recipients); paediatric liaison records.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Set the ED system to auto-copy every paediatric head injury discharge letter to the paediatric liaison inbox, which forwards to the health visitor or school nurse.
close_loop: Present to the safeguarding children group and ED governance. If it works, keep the auto-copy rule.
evidence: [449] local re-audit: GP letters for discharged children (registered)
[2627] vascular discharge letters: unspecified interventions did not cut delay (14.6 → 19.4 days; vague fixes fail)
[3595] psychiatry driving status: a template field lifted screening 25% → 85% (template field)
pitfalls: Letters generated but not sent → check the sent log, not the draft.
Health visitor contact unknown → route via the paediatric liaison team.
IT change takes months → start with a manual liaison list while the build is done.
Adults included by mistake → restrict to under 16.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric liaison health visitor as co-lead.
The safeguarding lead will back this; ask early.
Audit copy recipients, not just timing.
Keep a small weekly spot check after the change.
effort: ~10 min per 10 children from the letter log

question: What proportion of adults aged 65 or over discharged from the ED after a fall-related head injury are referred for a falls assessment?
why: NG232 (2023) added referral to investigate the cause of the head injury, such as a falls assessment. Falls audits in the library focus on inpatient checks [1685][1596] and GEM units [1880]; none measures onward referral from the ED.

standard.wording: Refer people with a head injury to investigate its causes and manage contributing factors, if appropriate. This could include, for example, referral for a falls assessment or to safeguarding services. [2023]

pass: Documented referral to a falls service, frailty team or GP falls review, or a documented reason why not appropriate.
population: Adults 65 or over with head injury after a fall, discharged from the ED or observation unit. Exclude admissions.
sample: 50 consecutive discharges over 2–4 weeks.
data_source: ED notes and discharge letter; falls service referral log.

change: Add a falls referral tick box to the ED discharge letter for patients 65 or over with a fall, which sends an electronic referral to the community falls service.
close_loop: Present to ED and older persons' governance. If it works, keep the tick box and report referral numbers to the falls service quarterly.

[1685] falls: huddle reminders raised lying and standing BP 34% → 68%
[1358] ED: electronic discharge prompt raised assessment 32% → 93.1% (discharge prompt)

GP letter wording counted as referral → define what counts before cycle 1.
Patients from care homes already known → record as 'already under falls team'.

Report CFS alongside to show need.
Show the number of repeat attendances with falls to motivate staff.
Keep the referral one click.

question: What proportion of adults treated in the ED for suspected anaphylaxis have two correctly timed mast cell tryptase samples?
why: NG258 (May 2026) repeats the timed tryptase rule. Missed or mistimed samples leave allergy clinics without a diagnosis. No anaphylaxis audit exists in the library.

standard.wording: After suspected anaphylaxis in an adult or young person aged 16 years or older, take timed blood samples for mast cell tryptase testing as follows: a sample as soon as possible after emergency treatment has started; a second sample ideally within 1 to 2 hours (but no later than 4 hours) from the onset of symptoms. [2011]

pass: First tryptase sample taken after treatment started, and a second sample taken no later than 4 hours from symptom onset, both with times recorded.
population: Adults and young people 16 or over treated in the ED with IM adrenaline for suspected anaphylaxis.
sample: 30–40 consecutive cases over the last 6–12 months.
data_source: ED coding and adrenaline administrations on EPMA for cases; lab system for tryptase sample times.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add a timed tryptase order set ('0 h and 1–2 h') to the ED anaphylaxis pathway, which prints two labelled tubes and adds a 1-hour task on the tracking board.
reaudit: After 3 months of new cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED governance and to the allergy service. If it works, keep the order set and copy results automatically to allergy referrals.
evidence: [2471] ED renal colic: order set raised calcium requests 77.9% → 94.7% (order set)
[1517] analgesia protocol: electronic order set 0/27 → 58% full compliance (order set)
[1673] VTE reassessment: timed EPMA prompt 0.13% → 74% (timed task)

Allergic reactions without adrenaline included → restrict to IM adrenaline cases.
Small numbers → use 12 months look-back and report as counts.
Second sample forgotten at handover → put the task on the tracking board.

Recruit the local allergy consultant; they want this data.
Pair with the auto-injector and referral audit to share case finding.
Build the order set once; it outlasts rotation.
effort: ~15 min per 10 cases from lab system

question: What proportion of patients discharged from the ED after anaphylaxis leave with two in-date adrenaline auto-injectors?
why: NG258 (2026 amendment) requires two in-date auto-injectors at discharge. Patients often leave with one or none. No anaphylaxis audit exists in the library.

standard.wording: At discharge following emergency treatment for suspected or known anaphylaxis, ensure the adult, young person or child has 2 in-date adrenaline auto-injectors (via a prescription, if needed) and knows when and how to use them, unless the anaphylaxis was due to a drug allergy and the drug can be easily avoided. [2011, amended 2026]

pass: Two auto-injectors supplied or prescribed (or two in-date devices confirmed), and training documented; or an easily avoided drug trigger documented.
population: Adults and children discharged from the ED or observation unit after suspected anaphylaxis.
sample: 30–40 consecutive discharges over the last 6–12 months.
data_source: ED discharge summary, TTO/EPMA, nursing notes for device training.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Create an ED anaphylaxis discharge bundle on EPMA: two auto-injectors as a default TTO, device training checkbox and an automatic allergy clinic referral.

question: What proportion of adults investigated in the ED for suspected pulmonary embolism have a 2-level PE Wells score documented before the D-dimer or CTPA request?
why: The Wells score decides between D-dimer and CTPA. Without it, CTPA overuse and D-dimer misuse follow. The library has one DVT algorithm study [1489] and no ED PE work-up audit.

standard.wording: If PE is suspected, use the 2‑level PE Wells score (table 2) to estimate the clinical probability of PE. [2012]

pass: A PE Wells score (number or likely/unlikely) documented before the first D-dimer or CTPA request time.
population: Adults 16 or over who had a D-dimer or CTPA requested from the ED for suspected PE. Exclude pregnancy and patients already on treatment for VTE.
sample: 50 consecutive patients over the last 4–6 weeks.
data_source: ED notes for Wells score; lab and RIS for request times and results.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make the PE Wells score a required field on the CTPA and D-dimer request forms from the ED, with the result steering the order set.
close_loop: Present jointly at ED and radiology governance with CTPA yield. If it works, keep the request field.
evidence: [1489] DVT: negative D-dimer plus low Wells safely excluded DVT and led to a revised algorithm
[1690] Ottawa rules: teaching lifted request compliance 43% → 57% only (education plateaus)
[1714] Ottawa knee: teaching 72.5% → 83.5%, not significant (request-form prompt suggested)
pitfalls: Wells written after the test → compare time stamps.
PERC used instead of Wells in low-risk patients → record PERC use as a separate field.
Radiology vetting already enforces it informally → check with radiology to avoid double work.
Required field filled with random numbers → spot check 10 scores for accuracy.
pearls: Report CTPA positive rate; it is the outcome consultants care about.
Recruit a radiology registrar to share data pulls.
Include the age-adjusted D-dimer question as a secondary measure.
Agree the form change with the IT team before cycle 1.

question: What proportion of adults with a likely DVT Wells score seen in the ED get either an ultrasound result within 4 hours or interim therapeutic anticoagulation?
why: Out-of-hours DVT presentations often wait overnight without anticoagulation. NG158 is clear about the 4-hour rule. The library has no audit of interim anticoagulation for suspected DVT.

standard.wording: 1.1.3 Offer people with a likely DVT Wells score (2 points or more): a proximal leg vein ultrasound scan, with the result available within 4 hours if possible (if the scan result cannot be obtained within 4 hours follow recommendation 1.1.4) ... 1.1.4 If a proximal leg vein ultrasound scan result cannot be obtained within 4 hours, offer people with a DVT Wells score of 2 points or more: a D‑dimer test, then interim therapeutic anticoagulation (see the section on interim therapeutic anticoagulation for suspected DVT or PE) and a proximal leg vein ultrasound scan with the result available within 24 hours. [2012, amended 2020]

pass: Ultrasound result within 4 hours of assessment, or a therapeutic anticoagulant dose given before the patient leaves the ED; or a documented contraindication.
population: Adults 16 or over with suspected DVT and a DVT Wells score of 2 or more in the ED or ambulatory DVT clinic. Exclude patients already anticoagulated.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 2 months.
data_source: ED notes or DVT pathway form; RIS for scan result time; EPMA for anticoagulant dose.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add a pre-printed interim anticoagulation line (DOAC or LMWH by weight and renal function) to the ED DVT pathway, triggered when no scan slot is available within 4 hours.
close_loop: Present to ED, haematology and ambulatory care. If it works, keep the pathway line and review it yearly with the anticoagulation team.
evidence: [1489] DVT: revised algorithm combining Wells and D-dimer adopted after audit
[2196] emergency surgery: drug chart checkboxes improved weight- and renal-adjusted anticoagulant dosing 29/36 → 37/38
[1358] ED immobilised limbs: pathway redesign with discharge prompt 32% → 93.1%

Keep the pre-printed line simple, with a renal dose table on the back.

question: What proportion of adults discharged from the ED or ambulatory care with suspected or confirmed pulmonary embolism have a validated risk tool documented?

standard.wording: Consider outpatient treatment for suspected or confirmed low-risk PE, using a validated risk stratification tool to determine the suitability of outpatient treatment. [2020]

pass: A named validated tool and its score recorded before the discharge decision.
population: Adults 16 or over discharged home from the ED or same-day emergency care with suspected or confirmed PE on anticoagulation.

data_source: ED or SDEC notes and ambulatory PE pathway form; discharge letter.

change: Add a Hestia checklist (or sPESI score box) as a required section of the ambulatory PE discharge form.
close_loop: Present at ED, acute medicine and respiratory governance. If it works, keep the required section.
evidence: [2093] hand trauma: electronic proforma uptake 95% and 11/15 items improved (proforma)

question: What proportion of adults seen in the ED after self-harm have a discharge or referral decision made without a risk score or a low, medium or high risk rating?
why: NG225 (2022) says risk tools and global low/medium/high ratings must not decide treatment or discharge. Many ED triage forms still carry SAD PERSONS or a risk rating. Library self-harm audits measured assessment times and completeness [3686][3400]; none checks use of banned risk scales.

standard.wording: 1.6.2 Do not use risk assessment tools and scales to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged. ... 1.6.4 Do not use global risk stratification into low, medium or high risk to determine who should be offered treatment or who should be discharged.

pass: ED record shows no risk scale score (for example SAD PERSONS) and no low/medium/high rating used to decide discharge or referral.
population: Adults 18 or over attending the ED after self-harm. Exclude those admitted to critical care.
sample: 50 consecutive attendances over 3–4 weeks.
data_source: ED clerking and triage forms; liaison psychiatry notes; discharge letter.

question: What proportion of adults with suspected TIA seen in the ED receive aspirin 300 mg before leaving the department?
why: Immediate aspirin cuts early stroke risk after TIA. ED patients are often discharged to a TIA clinic without a first dose. The library TIA work examined the pathway [1877], not aspirin timing.

standard.wording: Offer aspirin (300 mg daily), unless contraindicated, to people who have had a suspected TIA, to be started immediately. [2019]

pass: Aspirin 300 mg given in the ED (or already taken today), or a documented contraindication; referral to TIA clinic for review within 24 hours documented as a secondary measure.
population: Adults with a diagnosis of suspected TIA discharged or referred from the ED. Exclude those with intracranial haemorrhage or already on anticoagulants.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ED notes and EPMA administrations; TIA clinic referral log.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add an ED 'suspected TIA' order set that includes aspirin 300 mg stat plus supply for 14 days and an electronic TIA clinic referral.

question: What proportion of adults discharged from the ED with atrial fibrillation have a CHA2DS2-VASc score documented?

standard.wording: Use the CHA2DS2-VASc stroke risk score to assess stroke risk in people with any of the following: symptomatic or asymptomatic paroxysmal, persistent or permanent atrial fibrillation; atrial flutter; a continuing risk of arrhythmia recurrence after cardioversion back to sinus rhythm or catheter ablation. [2021]

pass: CHA2DS2-VASc score documented in ED notes or discharge letter, with an anticoagulation plan (started, referred or reason not).
population: Adults discharged from the ED with AF or flutter (new or known and not anticoagulated).
sample: 40 consecutive discharges over the last 2 months.
data_source: ED notes, discharge letter, EPMA TTO.

close_loop: Present at ED and cardiology governance. If it works, keep the template and include AF discharges in the monthly ED dashboard.

question: What proportion of infants with bronchiolitis seen in the ED receive none of the treatments NICE advises against?

question: What proportion of fluoroquinolone prescriptions issued from the ED have a documented reason why first-line antibiotics were inappropriate?

standard.wording: A patient's TCM should be administered according to their usual regime whilst they are in the ED

pass: Every Parkinson's dose due during the ED stay given (or self-administered and recorded) within 30 minutes of the usual time.
population: Adults with Parkinson's disease on levodopa or other time-critical Parkinson's medication who stay in the ED over a scheduled dose time.
sample: 30–40 consecutive attendances over the last 3 months.
data_source: ED system for arrival; medicines reconciliation; EPMA administration times; notes for self-administration.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'time-critical medication' question at triage that flags the patient on the tracking board and prompts self-administration or prescribing with usual times.
close_loop: Present at ED and medicines safety governance and submit to the RCEM QIP. If it works, keep the triage question and add a stock of common Parkinson's drugs in the ED.
evidence: [1165] Parkinson's inpatients: 86% did not receive appropriate medication in the ED
[1890] Parkinson's inpatients: 30% received all doses on time; education only
[2174] ED software mandatory field: 40% → 100% (triage system change)
pitfalls: Usual dose times not known → ask patient or carer and record at triage.
Self-administered doses not recorded → add a self-administration entry on EPMA.
Short ED stays with no dose due → exclude them.
Pharmacy stock gaps → agree an ED stock list with pharmacy.
pearls: Register with the RCEM QIP to benchmark.
Recruit a Parkinson's nurse specialist.
Use Parkinson's UK 'Get it on time' materials.
Report missed doses as counts; they are powerful at governance.
